necessary_conditions.content: M is a compact Riemannian manifold without boundary and the paper works throughout under the standing hypothesis that its dimension d is at least 2. Sphere statements also carry d at least 2, and the two appendix propositions restate d at least 2. The one-dimensional torus appears in Section 1 only as background for the classical theory, not as a case of the paper's theorems; no d = 1 version of the manifold statements is stated or proved here.

The admissible cluster is E_(Kn-K,Kn] built from sqrt(-Delta_g) eigenvalues in the half-open window (Kn-K, Kn], with K at least a constant K_0 depending only on the manifold. K_0 is produced twice, in the on-diagonal cluster bounds (775-784) and in the pseudo-distance theorem (797-802); the text says both can be assumed to have the same meaning only after increasing them (1061).
f_n belongs to the window subspace for every n at least 1, and the squared L^2 norms are summable, which is what makes the Gaussian process a well-defined L^2 object (Proposition 15).
M_s is a non-zero dimensional compact submanifold with smooth, possibly empty, boundary. It may be negligible for the Riemannian volume, for instance a closed geodesic.

For the non-Gaussian theorem the X_n are independent real random variables, independent of the uniform random vectors, with 0 < inf_n E|X_n| and sup_n E|X_n|^2 finite. Only these two moment bounds and independence are used; no symmetry is assumed for X_n, while symmetry is used for the random waves f_n^omega.

The uniform model draws a uniform vector on the sphere of the window and multiplies by the L^2 norm of f_n, giving a random eigen-wave of that norm; the Gaussian model divides the standard Gaussian coefficients by the square root of the window dimension, so its expected squared L^2 norm is also the squared norm of f_n.
The cut-off Psi maps [0,infinity) to [0,1], is smooth, equals 1 on [0,1] and 0 on [2,infinity); the invariance statement is asserted for any such Psi, hence for a fixed admissible choice.

quantifiers_and_regimes.content: The two-sided equivalence for the truncated sum holds for every N at once, with constants independent of N, depending on the manifold, the submanifold, K, inf E|X_n| and sup E|X_n|^2. Any restatement must keep N-uniformity; a per-N statement is strictly weaker.
Equivalence of the three numbers with a multiplicative loss depending only on the manifold, the submanifold and K; in the sphere case K is irrelevant.

The sphere cap statement compares with min(1, n delta_g) while the manifold statement compares with min(1, K n delta_g) because the manifold window has width K; the two are not the same normalisation and must not be merged.

For the sphere the equivalence is restricted to a closed geodesic ball of radius theta strictly below pi/2, since for even n the pseudo-distance vanishes on antipodal pairs. The manifold statement instead holds on the whole M.

quantifiers_and_regimes.item: scale zones in the manifold proof
quantifiers_and_regimes.content: Three zones: distance at least a fixed alpha; distance at least beta/(Kn); distance below beta_0/(Kn). The final theorem is obtained by taking the first conclusion with alpha_0 and the second with beta equal to beta_0, then increasing the constants.

Almost sure convergence in C^0, almost sure boundedness of the partial sums, boundedness in L^1 of the C^0-valued sums and L^2 convergence are all asserted equivalent in Proposition 23; the quantitative theorem is about the expectation of the supremum, defined via countable subsets at line 410.

The Salem-Zygmund condition is asserted necessary and sufficient in the manifold setting, in contrast with the torus where only sufficiency holds. Both directions are written: necessity at 1297 and 1697, sufficiency at 1299 and 1711.

The Gaussian wave and the uniform wave are linked through the chi factor chi_n and the contraction principle in both directions; the equivalence of the two models is asserted at the level of the L^2 norm of the supremum and of the expectation of the supremum.

recount_boundaries.item: shared core inside the same work
recount_boundaries.content: The two-sided entropy/weight dictionary (Proposition 6 and Corollary 7) is used by candidate C2 on caps, on curves and on the manifold, and is counted once inside C2 rather than as its own candidate. Corollary 7 is an immediate quantitative restatement of Proposition 6 and is not counted separately.

Theorem 1, Theorem 2, Theorem 3 and Proposition 23 are assembled from Propositions 15 to 22; their proofs reuse the same chi/Marcus-Pisier scheme, so none of them opens a new core beyond C2. They are preserved as statements but not counted.

Theorem 10 and its support (Theorem 11, Propositions 12 to 14, Appendix B) are reused under the old H2 without re-judgement. Candidate C1 is not a repackaging of that material: it concerns a single fixed eigenspace on the sphere, where the widening-of-cluster mechanism is unavailable, and candidate C2 is not a repackaging either, since it is the probabilistic equivalence rather than the pseudo-distance geometry.

The sphere-only statements of Theorems 2 and 3, the remark at 1665 that the Gaussian series is a chi-weighted uniform series, and the sanity remark at 405 on submanifolds are weakenings or comments of already counted cores.

author_unexpanded_or_open.content: The differentiated spectral asymptotic (Theorem 11) is declared known and not available in a published reference with a proof in the needed form; Appendix B is described by the author as elements of proof for a non-specialist reader, resting on the Canzani-Hanin statement and on Bin's Bernstein inequality. The reprinted Canzani-Hanin proposition at 2113-2121 carries no proof in this work.
Appendix B states that the argument relies on published references and gives elements of proof; it is not presented as a complete self-contained derivation.
The proof environment attached to Theorem 11 contains only a pointer to Appendix B, so the theorem has no self-contained proof at its statement site.

The introduction announces universality with respect to the random variables, to submanifolds and to the metric. Only the metric part gets a separate theorem (Theorem 5); the other two are consequences of Theorem 1 stated as remarks in Section 3, not as separate theorems.
The homogeneous-space reformulation for the sphere is given as a discussion using the orthogonal group and a non-Abelian Dudley-Fernique theorem noted in a footnote, not as a proved proposition.

shared_scope: Ambient M is boundaryless compact Riemannian, dimension d>=2. M_s has positive dimension, is compact and may have smooth boundary; do not extend the necessity statement to arbitrary sets or zero-dimensional samples.
For general M use the original spectral window (Kn-K,Kn] of sqrt(-Delta_g), K>=K0(M), and square-summable ||f_n||_L2. On S^d use single eigenvalue -n(n+d-1); K is irrelevant there.

Gaussian coefficients and the dim(E_n)^(-1/2) normalization are retained exactly. Almost-sure convergence in C0(M_s), existence of continuous versions and sample boundedness on a geodesic are different statements linked by the authored arguments, not silently identified.

The Salem-Zygmund expression is sum_p [p sqrt(log(p+1))]^-1 (sum_(n>=p)||f_n||_2^2)^(1/2). Preserve endpoints/indexing/log normalization; source subdivisions use reciprocal integer intervals, not a dyadic decomposition.

Theorem3 quantitatively compares E sup, the weighted spectral-tail sum and the entropy integral with constants depending on M,M_s,K, uniform under finite truncation. Preserve the countable-subset definition of E sup and open-ball covering numbers.

Sphere8/9 holds only on caps with theta strictly less than pi/2, uniformly in n>=1 and center. Even n has antipodal collapse; do not replace this by a global sphere metric equivalence or by a widened cluster.
